text:
CITATION
:

Yunger v. Zolty, 2011 ONSC
5943

COURT FILE NO.:
FS-09-352328

DATE:
2011/10/11

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE - ONTARIO

RE:
Reesa
Yunger v. Charles Zolty

BEFORE:
Justice
Herman

COUNSEL:

Rodica
David
, for the Applicant

Jaret
Moldaver,
for the Respondent

DATE
HEARD:
July 25, 2011

E N D O R S E M E N T

[
1
]

The
applicant mother and the respondent father seek various forms of relief.  The
mother asks for: temporary sole custody of the children; a proposed temporary
access schedule; an order that the father be restrained from removing the
children from Ontario; a restraining order; interim child and spousal support,
both ongoing and retroactive; special and extraordinary expenses; a
preservation order; security for support; an order that the mother be made an
irrevocable beneficiary of the father’s insurance policies; interim costs and
disbursements; the costs of a failed mediation; half of the funds in two joint
accounts; an order with respect to the questioning of André Zolty, the paternal
grandfather (“the grandfather”); disclosure of various items; and disclosure of
the father’s medical records.

[
2
]

The
father seeks: joint legal custody; a parenting schedule; an order that each
parent facilitate daily communications between the children and the other
parent; an order that the children’s passports be held in escrow pending
written agreement or court order; an order with respect to child support and
spousal support effective January 1, 2011; and a declaration that the funds the
father paid the mother in 2010 be deemed spousal support.

[
3
]

This
motion was originally scheduled for September 2010.  It was adjourned several
times. On October 12, 2010, Paisley J. made an order dealing with some of the
issues pending the return of the motion.  Most of the remaining items – but not
all – were argued before me on July 25, 2011.

[
4
]

At
the time of the hearing of this motion, there had not yet been questioning of
the parties; it was scheduled to take place in August 2011.

Background

[
5
]

The
parties were married on August 13, 2002 and separated in either March
(according to the mother) or May (according to the father) 2008
.

[
6
]

There
are two children of the marriage: Cindy Zolty, known as Tikva, born September
23, 2003; and Philip Gavriel Zolty, known as Gavriel, born May 30, 2006.

[
7
]

Both
parents are Orthodox Jews.  Their religion and their community pay a central
role in both of their lives and the lives of their children.

[
8
]

The
parties were young when they married: the mother was 19 and the father was 21.
During the parties’ marriage, they were supported by the grandfather while the
father undertook both Jewish and secular studies.  He has the equivalent of a
Bachelor Degree in Jewish Studies and an MBA in Finance.

[
9
]

The
father obtained full-time employment in sales and management at Supportive
Hearing systems in November 2008, that is, after the parties’ separation.  The
father remains in that position.

[
10
]

Prior to the parties’
marriage, the mother had taken two years of a diploma course in fashion
design.  Since separation, she attended a one-year course in interior design.
The mother says she has been searching for employment with no success but has
done a few freelance interior design jobs for minimal pay.

[
11
]

The mother commenced this
litigation in September 2009. Attempts at settlement and mediation were not
successful.

[
12
]

Each party views the
litigation through different lenses.

[
13
]

The father’s version is that
the mother is trying to extract funds from his family using threats, rumours
and the children.  He says the grandfather made it clear that his financial
contributions to the family would end if the mother disparaged the father in
their community, revealed her position for the reasons for the breakdown of the
marriage or pursued litigation.  According to the father, the mother did all
these things.  As a result, the grandfather stopped providing support to the
family.

[
14
]

The mother denies having
spread rumours about the father. Her version is that the father and his family
are engaging in a war of financial attrition against her: “you agree to our
terms or you will be cut off”.

Custody

[
15
]

The mother seeks an interim
order for sole custody; the father seeks an interim order for joint custody.

[
16
]

The mother says she needs an
order for sole custody to stop the bickering between her and the father.  She
points to two decisions that need to be made before trial that necessitate a
custody order: (i) the children’s schooling; and (ii) counselling for Tikva.

[
17
]

There is no disagreement
between the parents about religion or the children continuing to attend private
school.  The parties also agree that Tikva should receive counselling.  Rather,
to the extent that the parties disagree about education or health-related matters,
it is about who should pay.

[
18
]

The evidence before me is
that the parties’ disagreements relate primarily to parenting issues that will
not be resolved by a custody order, for example, concerns about Tikva’s
clothing or Gavriel’s weight, or to money.

[
19
]

In these circumstances, I
see no need for an interim custody order.  I would, however, encourage the
parties to seek the assistance of a parenting coordinator to help them resolve
ongoing issues related to the children.

Parenting Arrangements

[
20
]

The parties agree that the
children’s primary residence should continue to be with the mother.

[
21
]

The mother proposes a
residency schedule whereby the father would see the children on alternate
weekends, Wednesday overnights and alternate Monday evenings, with the
exception that Tikva would not necessarily spend the overnights with the father.

[
22
]

The father accepts the
proposed schedule with three exceptions: he wants to return the children from
their evening visits at 7:30 instead of 7:00; he wants one-half of holidays and
special days; and he proposes that Tikva have the same schedule as Gavriel.

[
23
]

The mother says 7:30 is too
late for the children’s return on a school night; the father says a 7:00 p.m.
drop-off gives him little time with the children.  I have no basis for preferring
one time over the other.  The evening visits will therefore end at 7:15 p.m.

[
24
]

The parties agree in
principle that they should share holidays and special days equally.  They are
in a far better position than I am to determine the best way in which to share
those holidays, whether it be on the basis of alternating years or splitting
the various holidays in half.   I would urge the parents to use their best
efforts to resolve this issue, failing which they may return to court.

[
25
]

The mother’s proposed schedule
provides for overnights for Gavriel but not for Tikva. The father acknowledges
that following separation, Tikva was uncomfortable with sleeping at his home.
In her affidavit of June 20, 2011, the mother says Tikva will now spend either
one or both nights on alternate weekends at her father’s but refuses to spend
any weekday overnights at his home.  The father blames the mother for the
problem; the mother says she encourages Tikva to stay at her father’s.

[
26
]

It appears that Tikva’s
willingness to spend overnights at her father’s has grown over time.  In these
circumstances, it is desirable that the two children have the same schedule of
overnights, with the exception that if Tikva is uncomfortable on particular
occasions, she should be returned to her mother’s home.

[
27
]

The parties agree that Tikva
would benefit from counselling.  They should attempt to agree to a counsellor
or therapist for Tikva.  If they are unable to agree on the name of the counsellor,
they will accept the recommendation of either Tikva’s family doctor or the art
therapist whom Tikva saw previously.

[
28
]

The father asks for an order
that each parent facilitate daily communication between the children and the
other parent.  I see no reason why it would not be in the children’s best
interests to have daily contact with each parent.

[
29
]

The father also asks for an
order that the children’s passports be held in escrow pending written agreement
or court order.  Given each party’s concern that the other parent may leave the
jurisdiction, such an order is appropriate.  There will also be an order
prohibiting either parent from leaving the jurisdiction with the children
without written consent or court order.

Restraining order

[
30
]

The mother seeks an order restraining
the father from molesting, annoying or harassing her, the children and members
of her extended family.

[
31
]

Section 46 (1) of the
Family
Law Act
, provides that the court may make a restraining order if the
applicant has reasonable grounds to fear for his or her own safety or the
safety of the children.

[
32
]

The mother says the father
has a “volatile temper” and sends her e-mails with demeaning and insulting
language.  The e-mails which have been produced relate to matters such as Tikva’s
clothing and Gavriel’s weight.  While the conflict between the parents as expressed
in the e-mails is unfortunate, particularly in so far as they relate to
parenting issues, I cannot conclude that one parent is more at fault than the
other.

[
33
]

The e-mails and the
father’s conduct, as described in the affidavits of the mother, do not rise to
the level that would justify the imposition of a restraining order.  The
evidence does not establish reasonable grounds to fear for the mother’s safety
or for the safety of the children.  I therefore decline to grant the order
sought.

Child and Spousal Support

[
34
]

The mother seeks interim
child and spousal support. Entitlement is not an issue but quantum is.

[
35
]

The father proposes that
child support and spousal support be $1,360 and $1,474, respectively, based on
his annual income of $96,439 and the mother’s annual income of $1,262.

[
36
]

The mother says that a
significantly higher income amount should be imputed to the father for purposes
of determining support.  She sets out several reasons for imputing income.  The
most significant reason is that the grandfather historically made substantial
contributions to the family’s support.

[
37
]

The mother also says that,
in the absence of more disclosure with respect to the father’s assets, it is
not possible to fix an amount.  She proposes instead, that on an interim basis,
there be an order for blended spousal and child support based on the mother’s
monthly budget of $11,900.

History of Support

[
38
]

The mother estimates that
she received about $10,000 a month from April to November 2008, based on her
withdrawals from the parties’ joint account.   From December 2008 to July 2009,
she says the combined payment for support and special expenses ranged between
about $8,000 and $9,300.  Between August 2009 and January 2010, the total
payments, according to the mother, decreased to between about $4,500 and $5,700
monthly.  The mother records no payments between February 2010 and April 2010
and says that between May 2010 and September 2010, the payments ranged between
about $3,801 and $7,400.

[
39
]

On October 12, 2010, Paisley
J. ordered the father to pay $25,000 to the mother, which payment would be
characterized later.  At the time the order was made, the motion was scheduled
to return to court in mid- January 2011,

that is, about three
months later.

[
40
]

After paying the $25,000,
the father limited his payments to about $740 for school fees up to June 2011.

[
41
]

According to the father, he
then paid the mother $2,291 in each of June and July 2011.   Based on the
amount of support he believes he should be paying ($1,360 child support and
$1,474 spousal support), the father says he has overpaid the mother $1,242
since October 2010.   The mother does not agree with the father’s calculations
of what he paid, nor does she agree with his position of what he should be paying.

The mother’s income and
expenses

[
42
]

In her most recent financial
statement, the mother has not included any income because she says any income
she has received is minimal and unpredictable.  The mother says she received
$1,407.79 in 2010 and $1,435.95 in 2011 from self-employment, before the
deduction of expenses.  I do not know what those expenses were.  For the
purpose of determining interim support, I will assume that the mother earns no
income at the current time.

[
43
]

According to her most recent
financial statement, the mother’s monthly expenses total about $7,000.  These
include 100% of the children’s school fees, although the father has been
contributing half.  The mother has received loans from her parents for legal
fees and other expenses amounting to about $188,000.

[
44
]

The father suggests that the
mother has made little to no effort to obtain employment.

[
45
]

The mother was 19 years of
age when the parties married and did not work during the marriage.  She says
she has looked for a job but with no success.

[
46
]

In the circumstances, I
decline to impute any income to the mother for the purpose of an interim
support order.  It is an issue that is best left to the trial.

[
47
]

The father also says that
the mother’s parents have means and if his parents are expected to help out,
her parents should help out as well.  The mother denies that her parents have
means.   I cannot determine whether the mother’s parents have means or not,
other than the fact that they have provided substantial assistance to the
mother since separation, particularly for legal fees. The mother has characterized
this assistance as loans.   It is, however, undisputed that during the parties’
marriage, it was the father’s family who provided for the family, not the
mother’s family.

Imputation of income to
the father

[
48
]

According to the father, his
total annual income is $96,439.  He says he has two sources of income: his
employment ($77,577.54 a year); and his position as an agent for a property in
Geneva ($18,802.40).

[
49
]

The mother says, firstly,
that the father is underemployed given his academic achievements.  The mother
did not, however, give notice to the father that she was seeking to impute income
on this basis.  In any case, there is insufficient evidence to enable me to
conclude that this is a situation of underemployment.

[
50
]

I therefore decline to
impute income on this basis for the purpose of determining interim support.  As
with the issue of the mother’s alleged underemployment, this is a matter that
is best left to the trial.

[
51
]

The mother also says the
father has interests in various properties which may provide a source of
income.

[
52
]

The father says he has or
had a relationship to three properties:

(i)
Pittsburgh property - According to the father, this property is owned by a
trust.  He says he was a beneficiary of the property at one time.  The
grandfather revoked him as a beneficiary prior to separation (although,
according to the mother’s date of separation, the change occurred just after
separation).  The father says the decision to revoke him as a beneficiary was
the grandfather’s to make; the property has no value at the current time; and he
has never received any distributions from the trust.

(ii)
Geneva property – The father says he holds this property in trust for his
father and he receives an annual management fee of about $19,000 for doing so.

(iii)
Canter Foundation in Geneva – The father says the grandfather is the beneficial
owner of the property; he only receives an interest after the grandfather’s
death.

[
53
]

On the basis of the limited
evidence before me, I cannot impute additional income to the father based on
these three properties.  The father has included the income from the Geneva
property for the purpose of determining support.  There is no evidence at this
time that he receives additional income from any other properties.

[
54
]

The issue, therefore, is
whether additional income should be imputed to the father either on the basis
of his historic financial contributions to the family or on the basis that
funds continue to flow to the father from the grandfather, notwithstanding the
father’s and grandfather’s assertions that the funding has stopped.

[
55
]

It is not in dispute that
during the parties’ marriage, their chief source of income was money provided
by the grandfather.  The father was in school, the mother was not working and
the grandfather provided them with $30,000 every three months.

[
56
]

The grandfather’s support
continued after separation, although the amount appears to have declined after
the father gained employment.  According to the father’s records, he received
$97,650 from the grandfather from February to December 2009, of which
$71,971.83 was spent for the benefit of the mother and the children.  In 2010,
the father says he received $103,840 from the grandfather, about $41,000 of
which went to pay his legal fees and $55,915.74 benefitted the mother and
children.

[
57
]

The last payment from the
grandfather that appears in the father’s record of payments was in July 2010.

[
58
]

The grandfather swore an
affidavit, dated September 7, 2010.  It states as follows:

I believe that I generously provided for my son and his wife, Reesa,
during their marriage and during a time when Charles was being educated.

I reduced my support when Charles was able to find an employment.

I have advised Charles that as of September 1
st
, 2010, he
will no longer be receiving monetary gift from myself or from his mother, nor
will we be paying any of his expenses other than travel costs to visit us.

We have been very clear to Charles that
we will not provide further
funds if they are going to be considered as income to him and used towards the
support of Reesa
, particularly when she has disparaged Charles in the
community and as she is using our money in effort to obtain money from Charles
beyond his means.  [underlining added]

I do not believe that I am under any legal obligation to support my son
or his wife.

I do, however, remain willing to contribute 50% of the costs towards the
education and counseling expenses for my grand children.

I am of the opinion that Reesa’s family may do the same.  They are not
people without financial means.

[
59
]

The father says he has not
received any financial support from the grandfather in the last year, with the
exception of monies the grandfather paid for the children’s s. 7 expenses, the
father’s legal expenses and the father’s trips to Switzerland to visit his
parents.  The father says the grandfather paid approximately 60% of the
children’s school tuition.  The grandfather also volunteered to pay for
Gavriel’s speech therapy.

[
60
]

The mother believes the
father continues to receive money from the grandfather.  She points to the fact
that he was able to come up with the $25,000 payment he was ordered to pay by
Paisley J.  The father says the money came from his savings.  He produced bank
statements in support of his position.

[
61
]

The mother says the father
is living a lavish lifestyle and must, therefore, be receiving assistance from
the grandfather.  The father denies it.  I have no evidence before me of a
lavish lifestyle.  The grandfather paid for the father’s trips to Switzerland.

[
62
]

Based on the evidence before
me, I am unable to find that the father is currently receiving funds from the
grandfather other than funds for legal fees, school fees and trips to
Switzerland.   I am also unable to find that the father has any control over
what funds he receives.  I therefore decline to impute additional income on
this basis.  If it is subsequently determined that the father is, in fact,
receiving additional funds, this issue can be revisited.

Analysis

[
63
]

I am unable to find that the
father is currently receiving support from the grandfather, other than targeted
contributions to legal fees and the children’s schooling.  The remaining issue,
therefore, is whether income should be imputed on the basis of the
grandfather’s historic financial support of the family, notwithstanding the
discontinuation of this support.

[
64
]

As a general proposition,
the grandfather has no obligation to provide support and the court cannot order
him to do so.

[
65
]

This issue was addressed by
the Court of Appeal in
Bak v. Dobell
,
2007 ONCA 304 (CanLII)
, [2007] O.J. No. 1489 (C.A.).  In
general, gifts are not considered to be part of a person’s income.  However, as
Lang J. noted at para. 74, there may be “circumstances surrounding the
particular gift [that] are so unusual that they constitute an ‘appropriate
circumstance’ in which to impute income”.

[
66
]

In determining whether it is
appropriate to include gifts in income, the court will consider a number of
factors, including: the regularity of the gifts; the duration of their receipt;
whether the gifts were part of the family’s income during cohabitation that
entrenched a particular lifestyle; the circumstances of the gifts that earmark
them as exceptional; whether the gifts do more than provide a basic standard of
living; the income generated by the gifts; whether the gifts are provided to an
adult child through a crisis or period of disability; whether the gifts are
likely to continue; and the true purpose and nature of the gifts (
Bak v.
Dobell
at para.
75
).

[
67
]

The issue was also
considered in
Whelan v. O’Conor
,
2006 CanLII 13554 (ON SC)
, [2006] O.J. No. 1660 (S.C.J.), a case
in which the court declined to impute income to the payor on the basis of
gifts.  After reviewing s. 19 of the
Child Support Guidelines
and the
cases, MacKinnon J. distilled the following principles:

1.   The court should be cautious in imputing income on the basis of
gifts when so doing would have the effect of transferring a child support
obligation to someone who, legally, does not have that obligation.

2.   Income is generally imputed where a parent is not properly
utilizing earning capacity or other resources to support his or her children.

3.   Factors supporting income imputation on the basis of gifts include:

a.

the gifts represent a
significant portion of the recipient’s overall    income;

b.

the gifts are part of a planned
or intentional diversion of income or substitution for income previously earned
from this source; and

c.

there is reliance upon the
regular and ongoing nature of the gifts as an income source in lieu of pursuing
other remunerative employment commensurate with the abilities of the
respondent.

4. Failure to make full disclosure is a frequent factor in cases where
income is imputed.

[
68
]

In
De Zen v. De Zen
,

[2002] O.J. No. 5827 (S.C.J.)
, the payor worked for his father’s business.
McWatt J. imputed income to the husband on the basis of her findings that the
father was intentionally underemployed, gifts from his parents made up for the
shortfall in his remuneration and the level of his income was tied to his
desire to control the level of child support he would be required to pay.

[
69
]

The court also imputed
income on the basis of monetary gifts from the payor’s parents in
Lo v. Mang
,

[2011] O.J. No. 390 at para. 103
.  In reaching his conclusion, Grace J.
considered the following:

1. The payments were not isolated or of short duration.  They continued
without interruption.

2. Mr. Mang made deductions for Canada Pension Plan contributions and
employment insurance premium.

3. The cheques were often signed by Mr. Mang and his sister.  There was
no indication that they sought or received permission.

4. The judge drew an adverse inference from the failure of Mr. Mang’s
parents to testify.

5. Mr. Mang acknowledged in his cross-examination that his
characterization of the monthly gifts as “temporary” was not true.

[
70
]

The circumstances in this
case are very different from the circumstances in
Lo v. Mang
and
De
Zen v. De Zen
.  In those cases, the contributions were ongoing.  In this
case, I am unable to find that the grandfather’s support of the father
continued after August 2010, with the exception of contributions to school fees
and legal expenses.  There is no evidence that the father had any control over
the grandfather’s decision to stop providing funds or evidence that the father
is entitled to receive additional income from the three properties.

[
71
]

The grandfather made a
conscious decision not to provide regular support to the father as of September
1, 2010.  He did not hide his reasons for doing so: he did not want any money
he provided to his son to be counted as income for the purpose of support to
the mother.  It would appear, then, that the father’s income has decreased not
as a result of a decision the father made, but as a result of a decision the
grandfather made.

[
72
]

The reality during the
parties’ marriage was that the family was largely supported by the
grandfather.  However, the law does not require grandparents to continue that
support.  While the grandfather’s reasons for his decision to stop providing
funds to his son may be distasteful, the fact remains that the court cannot
require the grandfather to continue to provide support.

[
73
]

The grandfather currently
provides the father with some payments, that is, for legal fees, trips to
Switzerland and a portion of the children’s school fees.  These payments are,
in my opinion, properly characterized as gifts, not income.  They are targeted
to a particular purpose; the father does not have any discretion or control
over how the money is spent; and the contributions do not replace income nor
are they relied on as an income source.

[
74
]

I therefore conclude that
the father’s income for the purpose of determining interim child and spousal
support is $96,439.

Quantum of Interim Child
Support and Spousal Support

[
75
]

Based on an income of
$96,439, the father’s monthly child support obligation is $1,360.

[
76
]

I have determined that, for
the purpose of determining support, the mother currently has no income.

[
77
]

The Spousal Support Advisory
Guidelines indicate the following ranges of support: $1,345 at the low end;
$1,553 mid-range; and $1,775 at the high end.

[
78
]

In my opinion, an interim
spousal support that is closer to the high end is warranted in view of the very
precipitous decline in support for the mother and the children since September
2010.

[
79
]

Interim spousal support will
therefore be $1,750 a month.

[
80
]

This order is without
prejudice to a subsequent variation or determination of child and spousal
support.

Timing of interim order,
retroactive support and attribution of funds to spousal support

[
81
]

As of what date should
interim support be ordered?  Should the father receive credit for what he has
already paid?  What amount should be attributed to spousal support in 2010?

[
82
]

The mother seeks child and
spousal support retroactive to September 2009 (the commencement of this
litigation), without prejudice to her claim for support retroactive to the date
of separation.  However, this would require determinations of what the father
paid, what the grandfather paid, what the mother withdrew from the joint bank
accounts, what the payments were for, what the father’s income was during the
period in question and whether the grandfather’s payments up to September 2010
should be included as part of the father’s income.  I am unable to make these
various determinations in this motion.  I therefore leave the determination of
retroactive support, if any, to trial.

[
83
]

The father asks that he be
given credit for what he has already paid since October 2010.  He submits that,
in the result, he has overpaid and does not owe the mother anything as of the
end of July 2011.  Of the almost $30,000 the father says he paid between
October 2010 and July 2011, $25,000 was paid pursuant to the order of Paisley
J. of October 12, 2010.

[
84
]

At the same time, the father
asks that I attribute $17,688 of the money he paid the mother in 2010 to
spousal support in 2010 so that he can benefit from an income tax deduction in
that year.  In arriving at this figure, he credits the same payment of $25,000.

[
85
]

Thus, in one chart provided
by the father, he attributes the $25,000 payment to his support obligations in
2010.  In another, he attributes the same payment to his support obligations
from October 2010 to July 2011.  It cannot be both.

[
86
]

Furthermore, it is not clear
whether the father has taken into account the required contributions to s. 7
expenses in his calculations.

[
87
]

While I am prepared to
characterize the $25,000 payment as combined spousal support, child support and
s. 7 expenses, I am not in a position to credit the payment to support owing as
between 2010 and 2011 or determine the portion of the payment attributable to
spousal support.

[
88
]

The interim support orders
that I have made will therefore be effective as of January 1, 2011.  The father
will be given credit for any payments he made on or after that date.  The
determination of credit for payments made before that date is left for trial,
where the judge will be in a better position to determine support owed and
payments made since separation.

Special Expenses

[
89
]

The major special expense is
the children’s private school fees.  The children’s attendance at a private
religious school is important to both parents.  The parties disagree, however,
as to how the school expenses should be paid.

[
90
]

The grandfather has
indicated that he is willing to fund 50% of the grandchildren’s school fees and
counselling expenses.  In his opinion, the mother’s family should do the same.
However, if I cannot require the grandfather to provide support, neither can I
require the mother’s family to contribute to school fees.

[
91
]

In most cases, the
allocation of contributions to s. 7 expenses is based on the parties’
proportional incomes.  However, the court may order otherwise (
R (EK) v. W
(GA)
(1997),
1997 CanLII 22798 (MB QB)
, 32 R.F.L. (4
th
) 202 (Man. Q.B.);
K.A. v. T.D.
,

2008 ABQB 222 (CanLII)
, [2008] A.J. No. 600 (Q.B.)).

[
92
]

In view of the grandfather’s
commitment to continue to contribute to the children’s school and counselling
expenses, the father’s contribution to these expenses is only partially funded
from his own income.  The mother has experienced a significant decline in
support as a result of the grandfather’s decision to stop providing funds.  I
conclude, therefore, that the father is in a better position to fully fund
these expenses than the mother is to make a partial contribution.  The father
will therefore be responsible for 100% of the expenses related to the
children’s schooling, counselling and therapy.  Any other s. 7 expenses will be
paid on the basis of an 80%/20% allocation as between the father and the
mother, respectively.

Preservation Order and Security
for Support

[
93
]

The mother seeks an order
for preservation of the father’s property and security for the father’s child
and spousal support obligations.  She also asks that the father’s support
obligations be binding upon his estate.

[
94
]

The mother submits the
following: the father is not a Canadian citizen and the children are his only
ties to Canada; he has no property in Canada; he has been secretive about his
financial circumstances; he claims an income significantly below what is
reflected by his lifestyle; and he has threatened to leave Canada.

[
95
]

Section 12 of the
Federal
Child Support Guidelines
states that the court may require that an amount
payable under a child support order be paid or secured.  Similarly, s. 15.2(2)
of the
Divorce Act
provides that an interim order may be secured.

[
96
]

The father says he has no property
to secure: he lives in rental property and he is not the beneficial owner of
any other property.  Based on the evidence before me at this point, the only
property interest the father has is in the Canter Foundation in Geneva, which
interest he only receives after the grandfather’s death.

[
97
]

The request that the support
payments be secured is therefore denied.  It is appropriate, however, that the
support obligations bind the estate, subject to any subsequent variation of
these orders.

[
98
]

The father consents to an
order that he not deplete any property, subject to his ability to withdraw
funds for his own support and to fulfill his support obligations.

Insurance Policy

[
99
]

The mother seeks an order
that she be made an irrevocable beneficiary of the father’s life insurance
policies.

[
100
]

This issue was not argued at
the hearing of the motion and is not referenced in the factums.  I therefore
decline to make an order at this time.

Interim Disbursements

[
101
]

The mother says she has no
assets, no income and no ability to fund the litigation or the necessary
disbursements.  She seeks interim disbursements as follows: $25,000 to retain
forensic accountants; $30,000 to retain counsel in Pittsburgh, Geneva and
Israel; and $311,000 as estimated costs to get to trial.

[
102
]

The purpose of an order for
the payment of interim costs or disbursements is to ensure that each party can
equally provide or test disclosure, make or consider offers and, if necessary,
go to trial.  In order to obtain such an order, the claimant must demonstrate
the following: the claimant is incapable of funding the requested amounts; the
disbursements are necessary and reasonable; there is a clear need for the
services of the expert; and the claim is meritorious on the balance of
probabilities (see
Stuart v. Stuart
(2001),
2001 CanLII 28261 (ON SC)
, 24 R.F.L. (5
th
)
188;
Biddle v. Biddle
,
[2005] O.J. No. 737 (S.C.J.)
.

[
103
]

The mother has not established
that there is a clear need to retain forensic accountants or counsel outside
Toronto.  In particular, she has not provided documentation from any forensic
accountants or counsel outlining what services they would provide and the costs
for those services.

[
104
]

The mother has, however,
provided an estimated bill of costs from her Toronto legal counsel.  The
estimated costs of $311,000 run from August 2009 to completion of the trial.

[
105
]

It is clear that neither
party, on his or her own, has the money to fund the litigation; each is
receiving funds from his or her parents.

I am not in a position to
assess the relative ability of the parties’ parents to fund the litigation.  The
father says the mother’s family is well able to help the mother pay her legal
fees; the mother disagrees.  The mother has thus far received $128,000 from her
parents for legal fees, which she has characterized as loans.

[
106
]

In any case, the father
clearly does not have the financial resources to fund the mother’s litigation
costs on his own.  Any order that the father pay the mother’s fees and
disbursements would be tantamount to an order that the grandfather pay.  I
therefore decline to make the order.

[
107
]

However, I am concerned that
the father may have substantially more funds available to him than the mother.
There is a danger that the father could use those funds to out-litigate the
mother.  I am also concerned that the mother’s estimated legal costs could well
outstrip any financial benefit she might gain from the litigation.

[
108
]

The parties should therefore
schedule a settlement conference as soon as possible with the objective of
determining how to most efficiently and economically move this case forward.

Costs of failed mediation

[
109
]

The mother seeks costs
resulting from a failed mediation; she blames the failure of the mediation on
the father.   The father disagrees with the mother’s characterization of why
the mediation failed.  I cannot make a determination as to why the mediation
failed and who was responsible, given the limited evidence before me.

[
110
]

I therefore decline to order
the payment of these costs at this time.

Proceeds of bank accounts

[
111
]

The mother asks for half of
the funds in two joint bank accounts as of the date of separation.

[
112
]

The father does not consent
to the release of the funds because he says the mother withdrew significantly
more than he did from another joint account.  He claims he is entitled to one
half of the difference between the funds she withdrew and the funds he withdrew
from that account.

[
113
]

The parties also do not
agree on the amount in the two joint accounts as of separation.  The difference
in their positions may be due to the fact that each party claims a different date
of separation.

[
114
]

The mother’s entitlement to
the funds cannot be determined in a vacuum.  I am not in a position to do an
accounting with respect to the funds withdrawn and the funds remaining in
various joint bank accounts.  That is a matter best left for trial.

Questioning of the
grandfather

[
115
]

The grandfather has sworn an
affidavit which has been presented as evidence in this case.  He has agreed to
be questioned.  The parties disagree, however, as to the mode of questioning.

[
116
]

The grandfather lives in Geneva,
Switzerland.  The mother seeks an order that either the grandfather attend in
Toronto for questioning or, if he is unwilling to do so, that he pay the costs
of the mother’s lawyer to conduct the questioning in Geneva.

[
117
]

The grandfather refuses to
come to Toronto for questioning.  The father’s position is that the questioning
should take place in Switzerland by way of Skype, and should be conducted by a
local judge or lawyer or by the mother’s counsel, as long as the mother funds
her counsel’s expenses.

[
118
]

Rule 20 (14) deals with the
questioning of a person outside of Ontario.  It provides that the court may
decide, amongst other things, the date, time and place for the questioning, the
person before whom the questioning will be held and the method for recording
the questioning.  However, the court cannot order a person outside of Ontario
to attend in Ontario for questioning under the
Family Law Rules
(
A.
v. B.
,
[2007] O.J. No. 5555 (S.C.J.)
, leave to appeal refused
[2008] O.J.
No. 504 (Div. Ct.)
).

[
119
]

The father proposes that the
questioning take place by way of Skype or other video-conferencing method.  The
mother is concerned that Skype is often of poor quality, there is a delay
between the question and the answer and it is not possible to discern who is in
the room while the deponent is being questioned.  She is agreeable to have the
questioning take place in front of a judge in Switzerland on the condition that
the father or grandfather pay the costs, including the costs of her lawyer’s
attendance.

[
120
]

I appreciate that
questioning by way of Skype or other video-conferencing technology is not
perfect.  However, I am mindful of the need to keep the costs of this litigation
at a reasonable level.  If, therefore, the grandfather will not make himself
available for questioning in Toronto, the grandfather will be questioned by
means of Skype or other video-conferencing technology.

[
121
]

The mother asks that the
questioning take place in English.  The grandfather’s affidavit was in
English.  The father did not indicate that questioning in English would be
problematic.  The questioning will therefore take place in English.

Disclosure

[
122
]

The mother asks that the
father produce the disclosure set out in Exhibit K of her affidavit, dated June
20, 2011. The father says he has provided the mother with extensive
disclosure.  Furthermore, he claims that the mother has not provided the
disclosure she was ordered to provide.

[
123
]

Questioning had not yet
taken place at the time of the hearing of this motion, although it was
scheduled to take place in August 2011.  The issue of the remaining disclosure
was not fully argued before me.

[
124
]

The issue of disclosure is,
in my opinion, better addressed after questioning and at a settlement
conference.

Production of the father’s
medical records

[
125
]

The mother asks for an order
that the father produce his medical records from Bellwood Health Services and
any other health care professionals relating to his sexual addictions.

[
126
]

The father denies that he
has sexual addictions.  He says he went to counselling in relation to this
issue because of pressure placed on him by the mother and her family.  He says
he is currently seeing a counsellor to help him deal with the difficult issues
arising from the marriage breakdown.

[
127
]

The mother submits that
disclosure of the medical records would assist in determining whether the
father had or has sexual addictions and why the marriage broke down.  I have
difficulty, however, in understanding how these determinations are relevant to
the issues in this litigation.

[
128
]

The mother suggests that the
father’s addictions may be related to Tikva’s difficulties with her father.
However, there is no evidence, at this point, that this is or may be the case.

[
129
]

The disclosure of medical
records is highly intrusive.  There are compelling reasons for preserving the
confidentiality of communications between the father and his doctor or
therapist.   In the absence of evidence that such records would be relevant to
any of the issues in this case, in particular, to the parenting issues, I
decline to order that they be disclosed.

Conclusion

[
130
]

My findings and conclusions
are based on the limited evidence before me.  I note that there are significant
issues in contention, in particular, the father’s income, and questioning had
not yet taken place at the time of the hearing of this motion.

[
131
]

No interim custody order
will be made at this time.

[
132
]

I would encourage the
parties to seek the assistance of a parenting coordinator to help them resolve
ongoing parenting issues.

[
133
]

The children will continue
to have their primary residence with the mother.

[
134
]

The father will see the
children according to the schedule proposed by the mother with the following
exceptions: the evening visits will end at 7:15 p.m.; Tikva will have the same
schedule as Gavriel, with the exception that Tikva will not be forced to have
overnights if she is uncomfortable; and the parents will share holidays and
special days on a 50/50 basis, according to a schedule to be worked out by the
parents.  If the parents are unable to agree to a schedule for holidays and
special days, they may return to court.

[
135
]

The parties will attempt to
agree to a counsellor or therapist for Tikva.  If they are unable to agree,
they will accept the recommendation of either Tikva’s family doctor or the art
therapist whom Tikva saw previously.  The parties will facilitate Tikva’s
attendance at and participation in counselling.

[
136
]

Each parent will facilitate
daily communication between the children and the other parent.

[
137
]

Neither parent will remove
the children from the province of Ontario without the written consent of the
other parent or court order.   The children’s passports will be held in escrow,
subject to the parties’ written agreement or court order.

[
138
]

The request for an order
restraining the father from molesting, annoying or harassing the mother, the
children or members of the mother’s extended family is denied.

[
139
]

The father will pay interim
monthly child support of $1,360 and interim monthly spousal support of $1,750.
The father is responsible for 100% of the expenses related to the children’s
schooling, counselling and therapy.  The father will contribute 80% and the
mother will contribute 20% to other s. 7 expenses.

[
140
]

This interim support order
is effective January 1, 2011.  The father will be given credit for any payments
he made on or after January 1, 2011.  The order is without prejudice to any
subsequent variation and any determination of support payable prior to January
1, 2011.

[
141
]

The request for an order
securing support is denied.  The interim child and spousal support obligations
bind the estate, subject to any subsequent variation.

[
142
]

The father will not deplete
his property pending trial, subject to his ability to withdraw funds for his
own support and to fulfill his support obligations to the mother and the
children.

[
143
]

The mother’s request to be
made an irrevocable beneficiary of the father’s life insurance policy was not
argued.  I therefore decline to make an order.

[
144
]

The mother’s request for the
payment of interim disbursements and fees is denied.

[
145
]

If the grandfather does not
make himself available for questioning in Toronto, he will be questioned in
Switzerland by means of Skype or other video-conferencing technology.  The
questioning will take place in English.

[
146
]

The mother’s request for the
production of the father’s medical records is denied.

[
147
]

Any remaining disclosure
issues should be addressed at a settlement conference after questioning has
taken place.

[
148
]

The following issues are
left to trial: support prior to January 1, 2011; credit to the father for
payments he made prior to January 1, 2011; the mother’s request for the costs
of the failed mediation; and the division of funds in the two joint bank
accounts.

[
149
]

I am very concerned about
the time and costs of this litigation.  The parties should schedule a
settlement conference as soon as possible with the objective of determining how
to move this case forward in the most efficient and cost-effective manner.

[
150
]

I would encourage the
parties to resolve the costs of this motion.  If they are unable to do so, they
may submit brief written cost submissions (no more than 3 pages in length plus
an outline of costs).  The mother’s submissions should be provided within 14
days of the release of this decision.  The father has a further 14 days within
which to provide his submissions.
